subject: humanities
passage: When films with recorded sound arrived in the late 1920s, cameras were so noisy that they were often placed inside heavy soundproof booths so that microphones would not pick up their whirring. Film historian Hélène Dubois argues that these booths, rather than any change in directors' tastes, explain why many early sound films have far fewer camera movements than the silent films made just before them.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Dubois's argument?

choices.A: Camera movement in films increased again soon after lighter soundproof covers let cameras leave the booths.
choices.B: Many directors of early sound films had also directed silent films earlier in their careers.
choices.C: Early sound films shot with cameras outside the booths had as few camera movements as films shot from booths.
choices.D: Audiences of the late 1920s often paid higher ticket prices to see sound films than to see silent ones.

explanation.why: Dubois says the heavy booths, not directors' preferences, kept cameras from moving. If camera movement came back as soon as the booths were no longer needed, the booths were the limiting factor.
explanation.A: Correct. Movement returned once cameras were freed from the booths, which shows the booths had been holding it back.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Directors' earlier careers do not show whether the booths or their tastes limited camera movement.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If films made without booths moved just as little, the booths would not explain the change, so this weakens the argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Ticket prices have nothing to do with why the camera moved less.
